subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: I used to be the loudest about Punjabi. When Hindi signboards appeared at the new bus stand, I ranted in the hostel corridor: "Nobody asks us. Why should we read theirs?" Noor, my roommate from Lucknow, was folding clothes and went quiet. Later she said, "Hindi is my mother tongue, and nobody imposed it on me. It felt like you were saying my language is the enemy." My face went hot. My love for Punjabi was real. But contempt isn't love; it was fear dressed up. I apologised that night and asked Noor to teach me a Lucknow proverb, and in exchange I taught her the first line of my favourite Punjabi folk song. We still swap words. Baljeet

qa.q: Where is Noor from?
qa.a: Noor is from Lucknow.

qa.q: What did Baljeet feel after hearing Noor's reply?
qa.a: Baljeet felt ashamed, with a hot face, and realised that the contempt had been fear dressed up, not love for Punjabi.

qa.q: Which choice by Baljeet repaired the friendship?
qa.a: Baljeet apologised that night and asked Noor to teach a Lucknow proverb, offering a Punjabi song in return, so pride and friendship could sit together.

qa.q: How did Noor feel about what Baljeet said in the corridor?
qa.a: Noor felt hurt, as if her own mother tongue was being called the enemy, even though nobody had imposed it on her.

grounding: A young adult loves the state language and bristles at signboards in another language, then sees that pride is healthy but contempt hurts a friend.

passage: Hostel warden's note, Sunday. Damini, 19, came to the office upset after a notice in the hostel was printed only in Hindi. She is from Kolkata and speaks Bengali at home. She said, "Nobody asks whether we can read it." I listened. She then added, "They should stop forcing Hindi on us," and her roommate Priya, who speaks Hindi, looked away. I asked Damini what she loves about Bengali, and she talked for ten minutes about poems and her grandmother's songs. I asked how that pride could sit beside respect for other languages. She thought and said she could ask the hostel to print notices in more languages instead of blaming anyone. She went to apologise to Priya, and they walked out together. Aditi, warden

qa.q: Where is Damini from?
qa.a: Damini is from Kolkata and speaks Bengali at home.

qa.q: Why was Damini upset, and what does her ten-minute talk show?
qa.a: Damini was upset and felt ignored by a Hindi-only notice. The ten-minute talk about poems and her grandmother's songs shows warm pride in Bengali.

qa.q: Which choice by Damini turned her anger into something useful?
qa.a: Damini decided to ask the hostel to print notices in more languages instead of blaming anyone, and went to apologise to Priya.

qa.q: How might Priya have felt when Damini said Hindi was being forced on them?
qa.a: Probably uncomfortable and hurt, since Priya looked away, and relieved when Damini apologised and they walked out together.

grounding: A young adult loves her state's language and bristles at Hindi being imposed, and learns that pride is healthy but contempt for another language is not.

passage:
First week. Manoj, nineteen, a fierce lover of Kannada, fumed at the new English-and-Hindi-only signboard in the college canteen. "In our own state!" he said loudly to his roommate Eshaan, from Lucknow. Then he added, "Hindi people come here and expect everyone to adjust." Eshaan went quiet.
Third week. Eshaan asked Manoj to teach him Kannada numbers so he could buy vegetables. Manoj taught him, grinning at his mistakes. That night Manoj felt a twinge: he'd said "Hindi people" as if Eshaan were a problem.
Sixth week. At the college Rajyotsava celebration, Manoj organised a Kannada poetry reading. Eshaan stood up and recited four lines, badly, bravely. The hall cheered. Manoj hugged him. "Sorry about what I said that first week," he muttered. "I love my language. That doesn't mean I have to hate yours."

qa.q: What did Eshaan ask Manoj to teach him?
qa.a: Eshaan asked Manoj to teach him Kannada numbers so he could buy vegetables.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling that night in the third week?
qa.a: Manoj felt a twinge of guilt for having talked about "Hindi people" as if Eshaan were a problem.

qa.q: What made the friendship grow despite the tension?
qa.a: Eshaan's willingness to learn Kannada and Manoj's patience teaching him showed that pride in a language can be shared across lines.

qa.q: How might Eshaan have felt when Manoj said "Hindi people"?
qa.a: Eshaan probably felt hurt and unwelcome, lumped with people Manoj resented.

grounding: Over several weeks, a young adult's pride in Kannada slips into contempt for Hindi speakers, and a friendship shows that pride need not include contempt.

passage:
Nilesh, you've been shouting on the internet about people who don't speak Marathi? Let your old Manoj Kaka tell you something.
In 1998, I was twenty, a student in Pune, and I was angry. Offices were putting up English-only forms; shopkeepers answered me in Hindi in my own city. I joined a group that marched for Marathi. Good. I loved my language, I still do.
But one evening in the group, some boys talked about "teaching a lesson" to a Tamil student who ran a small canteen near college. I felt sick. That student, Murugan, had fed me on credit for three months when my father was ill.
I left the group that night. I went to Murugan's canteen and ate there, loudly speaking Marathi, and he answered me in his broken Marathi, and we laughed.
Pride, Nilesh, is loving your own. Contempt is hating someone else's. Keep the first.

qa.q: Who had fed Manoj on credit for three months?
qa.a: Murugan, a Tamil student who ran a small canteen near college, had fed him on credit.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel when the boys talked about teaching Murugan a lesson?
qa.a: Manoj felt sick, disturbed that his pride in Marathi was turning into contempt for a friend.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Manoj's story?
qa.a: The turning point was leaving the group that night and going to eat at Murugan's canteen, choosing friendship over contempt.

qa.q: How might Murugan have felt when Manoj came to his canteen?
qa.a: Murugan probably felt relieved and welcomed, laughing with Manoj as he tried his broken Marathi.

grounding: An elder recalls loving Marathi fiercely and bristling at imposed languages, and choosing friendship over contempt for another language.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage:
The college fest's debate on "One Nation, One Language" started in fifteen minutes, and Ujjwal, twenty, still hadn't finished his speech. He was arguing against it, with every ounce of his love for Bangla. His draft ended with a line mocking Hindi as "a language without poetry."
His teammate Francis, from Goa, read it over his shoulder. "Ujjwal, you're arguing for Bangla. Why insult Hindi?"
"Because they're forcing it on us."
"Some people are. The language isn't. My mother reads Hindi poems to me. Konkani too."
Ujjwal stared at the line. The bell rang for the first speaker.
He crossed the line out and wrote: "Every language, Hindi included, carries someone's grandmother's lullaby. That's why none should be forced."
On stage, that line got the loudest applause. Francis gave him a thumbs-up from the wings.

qa.q: Where is Francis from?
qa.a: Francis is from Goa.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling when Francis questioned his draft?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt defensive and proud, angry that Hindi was being forced, and then uncertain as he stared at his own insult.

qa.q: What made Ujjwal's final line stronger?
qa.a: It kept his love for Bangla and his argument against forcing a language, but without contempt, which respected every language.

qa.q: How might Francis see the argument about languages?
qa.a: Francis sees that a language itself isn't the enemy, since his mother reads both Hindi and Konkani poems to him.

grounding: Under time pressure before a debate, a young adult's pride in Bangla nearly turns into contempt for Hindi, and a friend helps him keep pride without scorn.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: At the Pune college fest, the banner committee met in the canteen. "Why is the main board only in Hindi and English?" Vishal demanded. "This is Maharashtra. Marathi goes on top." Hemant, who had come from Patna in first year, shrugged. "Put all three?" "You people always..." Vishal stopped. Hemant's face had closed. The table went quiet. Vishal looked down at his notebook, full of the Marathi poems he wrote at night. "Sorry. That came out wrong. I want our language on the board. Not less of yours." Hemant rubbed his neck and nodded slowly. "Then teach me to write Swagat properly. I'll paint it." That evening the banner said Swagat in large orange Marathi letters, and under it, smaller, the same welcome in Hindi and English, in Hemant's careful brushwork.

qa.q: Where had Hemant come from in first year?
qa.a: Hemant had come from Patna.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when he demanded Marathi on top?
qa.a: Vishal felt proud of Marathi and resentful that it was left off, which made him bristle and nearly insult Hemant.

qa.q: What turned the argument around?
qa.a: Vishal noticed Hemant's face close, apologised, and separated love for Marathi from contempt for Hindi, which let Hemant join in.

qa.q: What might Hemant have felt when Vishal said "You people always"?
qa.a: Hemant probably felt hurt and shut out, as if lumped in with a whole group, which is why his face closed.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult's strong pride in his state's language, the pull toward contempt for another, and a friendship that crosses that line.
